utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We're grateful to counsel for giving an indication of the likely length of cross-examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Our general view is that it should be possible with this witness to keep cross-examination within the overall time-scale of the examination-in-chief, that's not so very far away from the estimates, it's probably a little less, but we would be grateful for that reason if you would try to tailor it to fit that rule of thumb. Good morning, Mr. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're going to continue with the cross-examination. Mr. Visnjic has just a little bit to go. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. We left off yesterday with the Defence Exhibit 3D487, in which General Ojdanic issued some tasks regarding the priority in the cases before the judicial organs. Now I would like to move to a different topic --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like the witness to be shown Prosecution Exhibit P930, if that can be brought up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is the Official Gazette where the law on the army was published, and I would like to ask you some questions about some of the articles in this law defining the purview of the General Staff and its chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Sorry. [Interpretation] P930

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this the wrong document, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think it should be -- I'm sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: 984, I'm sorry. Yes. Thank you very much. [Interpretation] Now I would like the witness to be shown page 2 of this document containing Article 5, and if we could perhaps zoom in on paragraph 1 of Article 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, Article 5 says that the General Staff is the highest expert and staff organ for the preparation and deployment of the army in peace and wartime. Do you agree with me that this is a provision in the law determining the rights and the powers vested in the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- something that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't answer that question. Mr. Visnjic, the law is in the document; and if you have questions about matters of fact that you want the witness to deal with, then that's fine, but we don't need him to tell us what the article says and what is law is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not mean to pursue this line of questioning. I merely wanted to determine whether Articles 5 and 6 are the articles regulating the role, the rights, and the powers of the General Staff and the Chief of Staff, and then I have some follow-up questions that I wanted to ask of this witness. I can, in fact, ask the questions right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, Articles 5 and 6, on the basis of what we see here, regulate the rights and powers of the General Staff. My question to you is as follows: Do you know that at the time when you were an active-duty serviceman that the Chief of Staff exceeded the -- his powers and rights, as described in this article?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about any such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to move on to a different topic. I would now like you to go back to the period of April and May 1999. General, do you know about the espionage case involving two Australian citizens?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us who those persons were, when, and where were they arrested, and more or less what you know about this case.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is known as the Prajta [phoen] case. When I was re-activated, this case had already been dealt with operationally. All I know is that sometime in late May it was made public that they had been sentenced. I think it was sometime on the 30th or the 31st of May. There were three persons that were indicted, and they were sentenced to jail -- to prison sentences of between four and 12 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know where and how they were arrested?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You don't know. Do you know if the diplomatic bodies of Australia were notified about their arrest?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know when -- where they were detained or remanded in custody?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in Belgrade in the military investigative jail, and that's part of the military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in the bodies where you worked or bodies that you contacted, was there ever any discussion or efforts to present these people as special agents infiltrated by NATO to assassinate Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No efforts were made to link them with any assassination attempts. They were tried and sentenced for espionage, nothing more. I don't know anything more about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were detained in some secret locations and that the military intelligence service actually had detained them in several locations and that their arrest and their subsequent detention was actually concealed from the public?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no secret jails. As I said, there was this detention facility in Ustanicka Street in Belgrade. That was the military investigative detention facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether in this case the military security service exerted any pressure on the prosecutor of the military district in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This service cannot exert any pressure on the judicial organs, the prosecutor, the court. I don't know anything about that. That's rather outlandish.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me read paragraph 13 of the Defence Exhibit 3D486. "One day in May 1999, the military security service arrested two journalists from Australia. They held them detained" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, what is 3D486?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a statement made by a Prosecution witness. This was disclosed to us, and this witness was supposed to give evidence -- he's supposed to give evidence before this Court sometime in late February. His statement is -- was made in September 2006, and I would like to check some of the information provided in this statement through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this witness has told you that he knows nothing of the circumstances of the actions of these people or of their arrest. Now, what is it now that you think he will be able to say to you? Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if we're going to discuss that witness or that statement, I would like to go into private session. There have been some recent concerns and a request for protective measures from that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Visnjic, we don't want to go through an exercise which is simply reading out something you know perfectly well the witness can't actually give any specific information about. You have to be in a position where you believe that he will be able to say something from his personal knowledge before it's appropriate to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I assume that witness held such a high post in his service; and in light of the importance of this case, I find it hard to believe that he did not have any direct knowledge of this case. And I think that he actually did share some of his knowledge about this case in the course of his previous answers, and his answers in fact clash with what is contained in paragraph 13 of the Defence Exhibit 3D486. I can explore this issue through this witness with a few brief questions, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The appropriate way to do this is to put specific points, matters of fact, and ask him what his position is on these, rather than to read out a statement. It's not the way to do it, and it's doubly not the way to do it when the witness involved may in due course be an appropriate candidate for protective measures. So please put the specific points you want to put to him until we see if there is any basis on which he's likely to give you any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I already have the facts that I need from this witness in the previous answers I got from this witness, and that is when those people were arrested, where they were held, what their status was, and whether there were any attempts or whether they were actually linked in any way with the ostensible assassination attempt on Milosevic. The witness answered those questions, and I simply wanted to put to him the whole story that was presented by this other witness in his statement and ask him of his opinion. If you don't want me to do that, then I can move on to another topic dealt with by this other witness, and this witness had already testified about this in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, you can put the allegation without reading out the statement. The statement's not his statement. If there's an allegation contained in it that you think this witness can deal with directly, then put the allegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've already gotten answers that I needed related to this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have an English hard copy of this exhibit that I can look at without the witness looking at it at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I see it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It's page 6, Your Honour, paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't see how reading this out is going to assist you. It's not even clear what's being said in the paragraph itself, whether this is a genuine case of -- or a case of genuine evidence of an assassination or whether it was simply a public relations exercise. What -- so you would need to put to the witness the basis for your proposition. Are you saying that this is evidence of a genuine assassination attempt, or are you saying that this indicates that it was all being dressed up as an assassination attempt?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this was neither an assassination attempt nor an attempt to dress it up as an assassination attempt. I think that the version of the events as painted by the witness in this paragraph is simply not true, and I wanted to hear this from the witness -- from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're not -- that -- I now understand you differently. You're not claiming this is the truth; you're claiming this is not the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you want this witness to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now I'm with you. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I am about to read a few sentences to you, and if we may have a comment on your part. "One day in May 1999, the military security service arrested two Australian journalists. They held them captive in several locations. Obrencevic told me in the presence of Gojkovic that it was decided by the state top" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Hannis, I forgot the point you made. Do you want this dealt with in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He is reading from the statement without identifying the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If it gets to a part where he's -- where it may reveal the identity of the witness, then I have a concern. If he says: My boss so-and-so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think that happens in this, does it, Mr. Visnjic? Is there a way of identifying the witness from what you're reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had no intention of mentioning the witness's name. In any case, I will try and avoid that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on then. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's not just his name, but if he references my immediate boss or my deputy, it could.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to meet all the conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I think I will have to re-start. "One day in May 1999, the military security service arrested two Australian journalists. They held them captive at several locations. Obrencevic told me in the presence of Gojkovic that the state top decided to portray them to the public as NATO special agents who infiltrated in order to assassinate Milosevic; however, the military security organs managed to arrest them." I conclude with the quote. My question, General, is this: Could you please comment on this part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any of it, apart from the fact that they were arrested and sentenced for espionage and subsequently released, I believe. They were pardoned, if I'm not mistaken. As for their involvement in an attempt of assassination and that there was a scheme in place so as to portray them as possible Milosevic's assassins, I don't think that has anything to do with it. In any case, they were mentioned in the media in that context when the spider or Pauk group was mentioned and another two foreign citizens were involved as well. I don't know if they were from Belgium or the Netherlands, and they were shown as someone who had knives in their possession and things like that but it has had nothing to do with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And it followed quite much later than the first case?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after the war had ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, another question about this exhibit. In the Milosevic case at page 16007, you described the case of Colonel Stosic -- Lieutenant-Colonel Stosic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I said "Colonel Stosic" because in this Exhibit 3D486, he's mentioned as Colonel; however, you said he was lieutenant-colonel. Was Lieutenant-Colonel within the security administration?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a very broad meaning of the word, he was in an organisational unit which was subordinated and part of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: Did the military security service try and cover up the case that Lieutenant-Colonel Stosic was involved in? Did they try to do that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what time-period you refer to. I mentioned Colonel -- Lieutenant-Colonel Stosic in my prior testimony as regards certain indications that some members of his unit may have perpetrated crimes in Gornja Klina; and within in that context, he was also in custody, there was an investigation in place, and proceedings instigated -- instituted before in the military court in Nis, but it was also concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the proceedings were conducted based on the information gathered by the military security service; this was the basis for the case?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I was in Glogovac on -- in the 37th Motorised Brigade, their security organ acquainted me with the Gornja Klina case, and we decided to arrest all of those people, including Lieutenant-Colonel Stosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you were in Kosovo, did you have any information about the military security service exerting pressure on the prosecutor of the Pristina military district concerning the case of Lieutenant-Colonel Stosic or any other case for that matter?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know why he would have to exert any kind of pressure on Stosic and what kind of pressure, what for?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no pressure. We detained him and handed him over to the appropriate military judiciary organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is this, General, pertaining to the period when you were not in active service just prior to the war: Am I right in saying that after the Rambouillet negotiations, the Army of Yugoslavia would receive information about NATO bombardment of Yugoslavia, irrespective of any further developments on the political plain?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such information in circulation, and I received one such piece of information and I acquainted the security administration with it. Do you mean immediately after Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, end February/early March 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness; however, I wish to tender -- I wish to tender several Defence exhibits that I did not mention to the witness. These are collegium documents of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. The Prosecution put forth a number of such documents, and we, therefore, wish to tender another number of such collegium documents following the same principle and on the same basis put in place by the Prosecution. Currently, I am unable to locate the list, but it includes three exhibits. By your leave, I'm ready to submit them after the break. I would provide the list of those Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to collegium -- VJ collegium minutes of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is, to some extent, unusual because in the course of the Prosecution case it would be not normally appropriate for the Defence to be presenting documents on a sort of free-standing basis that might be part of the Defence case. But in the exceptional circumstances I think where you could probably achieve that objective by simply asking the witness to identify these as apparently authentic documents from the collegium, then it's likely that the Trial Chamber will allow you to have these exhibited. But you can raise the matter after the break when we return.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, my name is John Ackerman. I represent General Pavkovic in these proceedings, and I have several questions to ask you about your testimony here. I'm sure you're getting very tired of being shown one document after another after another, and I'm sorry to tell you that it's not going to let up. I have several documents that I want to show you also. So with your understanding and patience, we'll proceed through that. Okay. Now, this has been discussed with you a bit. After the NATO air-strikes started in 1999, you told us that you made it clear that you were available to assist in any way you could and you actually wound up doing so; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you tell us how it came about that you actually did get re-instated in 1999. Did any of your colleagues that were on active military service assist you in any way in that regard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, we've actually had this evidence. I don't know if you've read the transcript of that part, but we had a detailed account from the witness of how he was approached to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I thought I'd read all the transcript, Your Honour, and thought that was not covered. If you say it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, if it's important to you to know the answer, but he, in fact -- I'm just trying to find where I noted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's more introduction than anything, Your Honour, I can pass over it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He was looked up by General Farkas and asked if he would accept re-activation and appointment in the republican state security with a view to obtaining some coordination between military and civil security. Is that an accurate summary, Mr. Vasiljevic, of how you came to be re-activated?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He nodded his head yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But if you need more details, please ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, I was under the impression that you had been assisted by some other members of the military at the time; and if that's not the case, you can just say so and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not assisted, and I did not insist on any assistance to be reinstated. Simply put, I and a number of other security officers who were retired were ready to lend a hand, to assist. We did not ask for reinstatement; we simply put our services at their disposal. I conveyed that to the people in the security administration. What followed was a call by General Farkas, and I believe it was in early April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is in the record, and thank you. I want to go now to some testimony you gave on the 18th of January, and I'm at page 8632 of the transcript where you were talking about the dismissals of Dimitrijevic and Perisic. You told the Chamber they were dismissed because of a disagreement with Milosevic, and these are your words: "With regard to the way Kosovo was being resolved." Now, I believe you took the position that Dimitrijevic and Perisic believed it was the job of MUP to combat terrorism and not the army; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They thought it was necessary for the army to participate, however, in the legitimate regular way once the emergency had been declared in Kosovo. They did not disagree with the use of the army but with the way it was being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And they were taking the position that the army couldn't be used unless there was a declaration of emergency by Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Milosevic, the Assembly was to -- supposed to put that in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, apparently, it was the position of Perisic and your position here last week that using the army to combat terrorism without such a declaration would be illegal and unconstitutional; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you'll probably remember Mr. Hannis even saying at page 8652 that members of the joint criminal enterprise that we allege in this case were aware that the kinds of actions they had been taking as far back as the summer of 1998 were in violation of the constitution. And I believe he's referring to that same thing. In paragraph 21 of your statement, General, you said that General Pavkovic may have earned Milosevic's favour in 1998 when he, Pavkovic, was willing to use the VJ in Kosovo in contrast to General Perisic, who was reluctant and who wanted a state of emergency declared. Now, again, I'm quoting from your words there. And in that context, you will probably recall that you were asked by Judge Bonomy just what it was that General Pavkovic did that General Perisic said required a declaration of emergency. Do you remember being asked that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And at page 8678 of the transcript, you answered Judge Bonomy this way: "What is he not allowed to do if a state of emergency is not declared, do I understand you properly? He cannot take the troops out of barracks. He cannot use armoured brigades that would support MUP forces in fighting the terrorist groups in Kosovo if a state of emergency had not been declared." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it might be helpful, General, to our understanding of this, if we would take a moment just to look at the law, and I would like you to look, please, at Exhibit 4D138. And the part of that exhibit that I'm interested in having you see, General, is paragraph 473. And what you have in front of you are the rules of service of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, these are the 1996 version of the rules. There is a Prosecution exhibit that is the 1994 version of the rules. These are more updated. 473 in this version I think corresponds to 450 in the Prosecutor's version of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if you'll look at paragraph 473 here in these rules, it says this: "Army units may be used to combat outlawed, sabotage, terrorist, and other armed enemy groups," and then it says in the second paragraph: "The Chief of the General Staff shall issue the order for the use of Army units to carry out the tasks stated in this item." You see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The registrar needs to turn the page. He can only see the first part of 473.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Do you require of me to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I don't, except to simply suggest to you that that would permit the Chief of the General Staff to order this kind of use of the army without any declaration of emergency from the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But in the paragraph before that, it reads: "Pursuant to the decision by the president of the Republic of Yugoslavia and the Supreme Defence Council." What the legislator had in mind was -- were terrorist groups, small groups. But if we are talking about an already-established illegal Kosovo Liberation Army and about a state of emergency in the territory of Kosovo, whereby almost all roads were blocked and they held a large portion of Kosovo in their hands by the Siptar terrorist groups, this is way beyond small, outlaw, and terrorist groups in the sense of this article, and even then it should be pursuant to the Supreme Defence Council's decision or the decision by the president of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say for certain, but I was not in active service at the time and I don't think such a decision was made by the Supreme Defence Council. The decision was made by the president without their approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't want to get into an argument with you about the law; but I suggest to you, there's a very important "or" in that paragraph 473. The first part permits the Chief of the General Staff to order the army against terrorist and armed enemy groups. The second part authorises him to do other things if there's a state of emergency called. But what -- I want to move on now. In 1968 [sic], when this dispute was going on, of course the Chief of the General Staff who would be referred to there in 473 was, in fact, General Perisic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an error. It was not 1968, it was probably 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, that was a mistake on my part. It was 1998.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Perisic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if these rules are as I suggest, General Perisic could have just simply issued an order for the use of the army in Kosovo in the way that he's apparently was complaining it couldn't be used?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He couldn't make any decision on the use of the army without the president's approval --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- or rather, an approval by the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look then at another document and this is 4D137.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I'd like the usher to come get a hard copy from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have one for you. And, General, I want to take -- I want you to take your time looking at this document. One of the questions I'm going to ask you about it -- in fact, the first question I'll ask you about it is if it appears to you to be an authentic document, and please take your time looking at it because I will have several questions about it.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it seems to be authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It has the seals; it has the signature of General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's dated 28 July 1998?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At the very beginning of that document under the heading "directive," it says the directive is: "To deploy the Yugoslav army for securing the state border with Albania, units and facilities in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and crush the armed rebel forces." Correct? Is that what that says?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not in dispute. Evidently, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, what's the difference between a directive and an order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An order refers to the use of smaller units, as compared to a directive, which refers to the use of strategic groups. An order is used at lower levels, subordinate levels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, General, if we go to paragraph III of this document now, and I think that is on page 2 for you, you see that General Perisic sets out various stages of this engagement. And in the first stage, he talks about what's to take place in the zone of the Pristina Corps and the protection activities the army is to engage in there, and then says this: "Through quick actions coordinated with the forces of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, overwhelm and destroy the sabotage and terrorist forces in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, as per a special order from the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army." And if you go on down to "tasks for the 3rd Army," paragraph 2.1: "Through quick actions coordinated with the forces of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, overwhelm and destroy the DT, sabotage and terrorist forces, in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, as per a special order from the Yugoslav Army's General Staff." So doesn't it appear that what General Perisic is doing here on the 28th of July, 1998, is ordering exactly what he claimed was unconstitutional, illegal, for him to do?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm commenting now on something that I should study in greater detail, but I will do so based on my scanning this document. First of all, it's not clear pursuant to whose order and whose standpoint this directive was drawn up. Usually, it says pursuant to a decision of the president of Yugoslavia, for instance, or pursuant to decisions reached at such and such a session. Usually, such a directive on the use of armed forces requires that kind of introduction to be implemented in practice. Secondly, this speaks about the use of the army to secure the state border; but as far as I know, there was a wider belt encompassing the state border. Previously, it had been a hundred metres wide, but later it was broadened to several kilometres, if I'm correct. So this is the area of the state border with Albania, and it also includes units and facilities in that area. The third part refers to crushing and breaking up the forces of the armed rebellion. These are activities outside the border belt. This is all beyond dispute, but I do not see pursuant to what this decision was made because it's common knowledge who can issue a decision on the use of the army. At the time I did have some information and knowledge. It was the army that was proposing this way of using the army. It's also beyond dispute that Perisic advocated this kind of use of the army; but as far as I know, he and Dimitrijevic wanted a state of emergency to be declared because objectively it did exist in Kosovo. So it just had to be openly stated, and this would then enable the army to act in different conditions. Now the army is being deployed in the border belt, which is what it is meant to do; however, if there is an escalation, if a mobilisation is required, then the army activities spread over a wider area. That's my interpretation of all this. I did not, myself, participate in these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, General, this directive clearly deals with deployment of the army beyond the border belt. The paragraphs that I read to you talks about deploying the forces on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, not just in the border belt. "To overwhelm and destroy the terrorist forces in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija." That's the entire country, and that is what Perisic is ordering here. And this is what the Prosecution has contended and you have contended would have been unconstitutional for him to do. Now, as per the authority, I just showed you that, the Rules of Service 473, which says clearly that he can issue this order, and based on that I suggest to you that's what he did.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you what the tasks are in 2, 2.1, 3. This is the first stage and units that are ready are mentioned up to 1800 hours. It says strengthen in-depth securing of the border belt in the area of the Pristina Corps, protect the units and military facilities from any activities from sabotage groups, and secure that the supply routes to the units are safe and passable. This is all directly linked to the area that the army was in charge of and the protection of its own facilities. That's the first stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the next paragraph that's important. The next paragraph makes it province-wide, Kosovo-wide, takes in everything, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The one after the one you were just reading: "Through its presence and" -- no, no, that's not it. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second stage, it says: "Carry out mobilisation," but it's well-known who can order mobilisation. It's not the Chief of the General Staff; it's higher-ranking organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, in -- I read those paragraphs to you twice now, and I'm not going to read them again. It's clear that the order was to combat terrorism throughout the entire Kosovo and Metohija. I want to move on. In the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, before you do, is the reference in this document, which is difficult to read the whole of when it's on e-court, to the troops supporting or being used in support of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's in -- it's on page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Paragraph number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, right at the very top: "Through quick actions coordinated with the forces of the MUP" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have page 3 of the English, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not it. Maybe it's at the top of that, go to the top of that page. There it is. "Through quick actions coordinated with the forces of the MUP..." and then you see the same action closer to the bottom: "Through quick actions coordinated with the forces of the MUP..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, assuming this order was regularly issued by General Perisic, I take it that in the normal course of events -- well, first of all, I must ask you. This order was -- you'll see on it, it was directed to the 3rd Army, was it not, among other -- on the last page?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I assume in the normal course of events that then one would expect that an order would have gone out from the 3rd Army implementing this directive from General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I may interpret this directly. On the first page in the upper right-hand corner, it says: "Defence, state secret-R," and then there is a code number. These are documents pertaining to the war plan. This is a document of war planning, how something would develop. This is not an executive order to be implemented right away. The subordinate commands, when they receive a directive such as this, then they draw up their own documents based on this. But the decision for the army to act on this as far as I can understand the situation and the rules, such a decision cannot be issued by the General Staff and the Chief of the General Staff bypassing the institution superior to him, primarily the president of the state and the Supreme Defence Council. The council presents the president with its standpoints on the deployment of the army. So this is an element of war planning and preparation for a certain situation. And, probably, this would be accompanied by maps with the elements entered into them, and also we don't see here who has approved this. This was done by the General Staff; but to the best of my knowledge, the president of Yugoslavia would have to give his approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well -- and you don't have any knowledge about that at all. I want to show you 4D140 now, and I also have a hard copy for you because it's a long document. Now, first thing I want you to do is look at it and confirm that it's an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It looks authentic in view of its form and content.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And now, this document is an order issued by General Samardzic and it's on the same -- the next day, the 29th of July, 1998, and I think you will notice that a copy of that went to the Pristina Corps. And I suggest to you what this is is an implementation by order, as you suggested would be the next step, of the directive issued by General Perisic that we just looked at.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we look at GROM 98, this is an order to smash forces, but it would require a more detailed reading and an expert will probably be able to do this more thoroughly. The stages are provided for here, but there is no date saying when mobilisation is to begin. So these are preparatory elements so that when such a decision is issued, the army has its plans ready. So the activities here are planned by stage, but no time-frame is provided. Let me see when reports have to be delivered. You can't see when this enters into force. You can only see when it was drawn up, the 29th of July, pursuant to what the General Staff issued previously, its directive. So the people in the 2nd Army in Montenegro and everybody else who received a directive drew up such documents, documents such as this one. This is an element of war planning and preparation for combat, but the actual decision to act on the plan has to be made by the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This document, I'm looking at the English part. It's in section 2 that says "army tasks," and I think you'll find that on page 3 of your document. In the second paragraph it says: "In a coordinated action with the Serbian MUP forces, launch rapid attacks to smash and destroy DT forces in Kosovo and Metohija in accordance with the special order of the Chief of the General Staff." On page 5 of the English, and it would be 3.5, and that would be page 5 of your document, where General Samardzic says: "I have decided to engage," in other words, he's now making a decision to engage. "I have decided to engage part of the permanent army force, reinforced by other VJ units," and then right underneath that paragraph: "based on a special order issued by the VJ General Staff in coordinated action with Serbian MUP forces, launch rapid and energetic attacks to smash and destroy DT forces in Kosovo and Metohija and in the Pecinja district." That's what it says, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I maintain what I said before. This is an element of preparation. This is the planning stage for combat which is yet to be implemented. The decision to implement the order when it becomes an executive order and the time-frame are missing. There are war plans saying in the same way: If there is an aggression from this or that side, the units will be deployed in such and such a way. But it doesn't mean that this has entered into force. So for this to enter into force a special decision has to be issued, and I've already told you who can issue it. As far as I know - and my knowledge is fragmentary and partial - this was the only matter in dispute. There is no dispute that Perisic and Samardzic agreed to the use of the army as planned, but it was the competent organ that had to issue the decision and a state of emergency had to be declared. They felt that a situation of emergency already did exist in Kosovo, but it had to be formally declared for the plan to be implemented. This decision was not issued, and that was the reason for the dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We're still over there on page 5 of the document, and you keep telling me that it's not implemented. And I suggest to you when he says: "I have hereby decided to engage part of the permanent army force," and set out how it is to be engaged, that that is the implementation. And if you will look on the next page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before you go to the next page, what I understand the witness to be saying is, if you look at the next paragraph of 4, that before action can actually be taken there has to be a special order issued by the VJ General Staff, and that's special referred to in the first line of that next section.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure what that means, Your Honour, but if we go over --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It does mean that there ought to be a special order. And if your case is right, the special order would be issued on the 28th of July. And if your case -- and if the witness's case is right, the special order may never have been issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it was the 28th of July issue, because you see where we're going next, Your Honour. If we go to the next page we get down to a section that says: "Operational deployment," then underneath that a section that says: "Stand-by." And in that stand-by section, it actually has a date of deployment, and that is 6 August at 0500 hours for smashing and destroying DTG, so like a week after the issuance of this order it was supposed to be made effective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's ask Mr. Vasiljevic. You see the reference there to the date, the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's on page 6, General, near the top.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, you see, this is to secure the passability of communications. The date is the 6th of August; but everything else, destroying the DTS, that's in accordance with the special order. And for destroying armed rebellion forces by engaging mobilised units in M + 12, that means in 12 days after mobilisation or at 1200 hours. I'm not sure what this refers to. M is the moment when mobilisation is carried out. So it's one thing to ensure road passability for roads normally used by the army, even in peacetime, but that's only on the 6th of August. But for the deployment of the units, a special order would be issued. So I'm just trying to explain that to the best of my understanding, as this has a code name, GROM 98, this is an element of war planning. Even now in peacetime, there are well-developed planning pertaining to particular situations; but when they will enter into force, that depends on the Assembly declaring a state of war, mobilisation, and so on. At that time it was the Supreme Defence Council that had to issue such decisions. How could these -- if this is an executive order on the 29th of July, how could then the road passability be ensured only on the 6th of August? That's the first thing that has to be done to ensure road passability before anything else is implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I suggest to you, General, that reading part of that sentence it doesn't just say ensuring road passability. It says: "And smashing and destroying DTG," that's the terrorist elements?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, that must be read along with the next line. The witness is reading it as: "Ensuring road passability and smashing and destroying DTG." In other words, create the situation where that can be done, because it's the next line that says: "For destroying DTS in accordance with the special order." I'm not clear what the difference between DTS and DTG is, but I suspect that's a mistran.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It may be, Your Honour, but I think in any event we have exhausted what we can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the point is clear to the Trial Chamber. The one is now a question of interpretation based on all the evidence we'll ultimately hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And we'll no doubt hear more about these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, thank you. We're going to go on now to another place. One thing that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There are a couple of things that I do want to point out, Your Honours, before I move on. First of all, I just make the assertion that nowhere in either of these directives or orders does the -- do the words "Joint Command" appear. And the second thing that I think is significant is the Perisic order that is dated the 28th of July was issued five days after the Perisic letter that we've seen in this case to Milosevic, which I think was dated 24th of July, and that's P717. And I'm not going to go into in any more detail than that, just in the interests of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's helpful, Mr. Ackerman. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, there's been talk about Mr. Perisic being -- General Perisic being basically fired, replaced, whatever, because of a disagreement with Milosevic and his contention that it was illegal to issue this kind of directive that we've just seen here today. The fact is that he wasn't really fired; he was offered the position of assistant minister of defence, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are just some nuances. If a military serviceman is appointed to a post such as that of an advisor or assistant which doesn't exist in the establishment itself, this is a way to remove this person from the leadership position in a quiet way. He was marginalised, and this is what was done to General Dimitrijevic. They were removed from their posts, but the impression that was -- tried to -- the impression that they wanted to achieve was that they were not really replaced but they were given some other post. But this is nothing really -- this is not something that can be contested. The same thing happened to General Velickovic in the air force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So your answer to my question was yes?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were removed from their post. They were forced to leave. Let me put that in clear terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're not listening to me. I didn't ask you about any "theys." I said: "Perisic was not fired; he was offered the position of assistant minister of defence." Now, you could just say "yes" if that's true.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not true; that's a half truth. He was offered this post, but the first element is that he was removed from his post.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, of course he wouldn't be offered the new one if he wasn't removed from the first one. But the answer is he was offered that post of assistant minister of defence, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, that wasn't hard, was it? That could have been answered with a "yes" a long time ago, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Well, I will try to be briefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 19 of your statement you say this: "However, the chain of command was often circumvented by General Pavkovic going directly to Milosevic without the knowledge or authorisation of General Ojdanic. It was Ojdanic's opinion that Sainovic and the Joint Command were receiving more information than he was." Now, you were asked about this by Mr. Hannis at page 8669 of your testimony and asked for examples of Pavkovic going directly to Milosevic. And the only one you came up with was when you actually saw Pavkovic leaving Milosevic's office on that day in May; correct? In June, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In mid-June, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you have no idea the subject of a meeting between Milosevic and Pavkovic that day, if in fact one happened, do you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is clear that a meeting took place. Milosevic confirmed that Pavkovic had been to see him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not the question. I really insist that you listen to my question. My question is: You don't know the subject of a meeting that went -- if a meeting took place between Milosevic and Pavkovic that day, you don't know the subject of that meeting, do you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you do question the very existence of the meeting. You are asking me two questions wrapped up in one. So your first putting to question the fact that the meeting existed, and I'm telling you that Milosevic confirmed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Milosevic said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Milosevic said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, please. The only question that you were asked, Mr. Vasiljevic, was that you didn't know the subject of a meeting that went on. Now, is your answer to that yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know what the topic discussed at the meeting was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the additional point you're anxious to convey to us is that Milosevic said that he and Pavkovic had a meeting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I wanted to say, since the question itself contained the phrasing "if there was a meeting at all." So the very existence of the meeting was brought into question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what Milosevic said about that meeting was that it was not an official meeting, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in paragraph 21 of your statement, you even indicated your understanding that there was some kind of a family connection between General Pavkovic and Milosevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know, don't you, that under the Rules of Service of the Yugoslav Army that it's perfectly permissible for the commander-in-chief to have conversations with members of the army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And as far as you know, General Pavkovic was certainly operating within the chain of command by making regular reports up the chain of command, as required, and following orders coming down the chain of command as he received them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that to a certain extent, but I can't go into details. I know that as a general rule he did carry out his tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at another exhibit, it's 4D136.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not give you a full answer because I only gave you a yes or no answer to the right of the superior to communicate directly with his subordinates. You are right there; but in such a situation, the subordinate is duty-bound to inform about the conversation to his superior, either before or after such a conversation, regardless of the fact that he had been summoned by an even more superior organ. General Pavkovic was duty-bound to inform the Chief of Staff about any such meetings. He failed to do so, and General Ojdanic's comment was to that effect. He was taken aback by that, and he told Milosevic: "This is not a problem. You can summon my subordinates to you, but please do not do that without me knowing about that."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And maybe that was when Milosevic said this was not an official meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was his comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want you to look now at 4D136.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I'd like the registrar just to page through it slowly so that the witness can look at it. It should be on your screen now. And we'll page through it just one page at a time, rather slowly, so that you can get a sense of what it is. Next page, please. There we go. We seem to have gone all the way to the final page at this point. I guess that is the final page, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what this is?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the official assessment, the evaluation of active officers in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this one is the evaluation and assessment of General Nebojsa Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was made by the commander of the 3rd Army, General Samardzic, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And assessing his performance from 29 June 1997 to 10 January 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't see the date; but if you see it, I see no reason why I should disagree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We would have to go back to the first page for you to see it, but I'll tell you that's what it is. If we look at the last page, the written assessment, it talks about him holding the post of commander of the 3rd Army of the Pristina Corps. At this post he showed superior qualities, that he had been continuously improving on over time as a result of several previously held posts. And it goes on with fairly significant praise of the results achieved by General Pavkovic and his assessment is exceptional. Is there any assessment higher than exceptional, General?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's the highest assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I want you to look now at another document, this is 4D121.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm unsure when it is we break on these days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 10.45, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this is a document dated 13 April 1999, and it's a combat report to the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army from the 3rd Army command. And at that time, the 3rd Army commander was General Pavkovic and the Chief of the General Staff was General Ojdanic. The part of that that I am primarily interested in is under section 2.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I think we need to go in the English to page 3. And in the -- we're going to have to go one more page in the English. There. I think that's it. And in the Serbian I'm not sure what page it's on, but I think it's maybe on the second or third page. Let's see if we can peruse through the Serbian part here. I think it's the next page. Yeah, that will do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right above where it says paragraph 2.2, you'll see a paragraph reporting criminal activity that had been referred to the military prosecutor's office. "Six criminal reports, five requests for investigation, seven indictments, one non-commissioned officers, three privates, and three non-serving civilians." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could we have the English version of this on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It should be -- it's right at the bottom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes. We've got it right at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- and it carries over to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could we go over the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then can we go to the final page. Keep going. There we go. And the same with the B/C/S. The part I'm interested in the B/C/S may be -- I think it's probably there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You see the language that says: "In view of the build-up of air, naval, and land forces in the neighbouring countries, it is only to be expected that NATO air forces and PS will continue to engage military units, facilities, and civilian infrastructures in Kosovo and Metohija as their primary target and at the same time make preparations for a land operation." So it appears at this point the army was certainly preparing for and expecting a land operation by NATO with land forces coming into Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm through with that document now. I'll go to document 4D9 -- wait a minute. 4D122.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Be sure you need the document because certainly your last question could have been asked without the document and answered I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It could have, Your Honour. It was just convenient with the document already there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because this operation definitely slows us down a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, Your Honour, 4D122 is the same kind of a report. It's dated 29 April 1999. It's from General Pavkovic to the General Staff. And on page 2 of this document, right before paragraph 3, it provides this report: "The military prosecutor's offices received 116 criminal reports. Three officers, 34 privates, and 79 outside VJ civilians contracted to provide services to the army. Two requests for investigation, an officer and a private. Indictments against eight privates. Four persons detained, eight requests for investigation, ten indictments, and seven adjudicated cases."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So again General Pavkovic is reporting the crime situation up to General Ojdanic, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is just an overview --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- a general report about the cases that were instituted - please allow me - but you cannot see what offences were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right. You can simply see that they're being prosecuted and dealt with. I want to look now -- I'm trying to move as rapidly as possible, General, without creating confusion. I want to go to 4D99. 4D99 is a report from the General Staff to the Pristina Corps, apparently. And it's simply reporting that Chief of the General Staff, Colonel-General Perisic, will come to Kosovo and make an inspection tour of the forces engaged there between the 10th and the 13th of August, 1998. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if -- if we follow the date path that we've been on today, we have the directive from Perisic of the 28th of July, the follow-up order of General Samardzic of the 29th of July, the directive in there that some matters are certainly required to be initiated on the 6th of August, then there's this report that comes out on the 7th of August, saying that General Perisic is now going to come down and take a look at how things are going there. It appears as if he has expected his directive to be carried out and is coming down to see how it's being carried out. Doesn't that make sense?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot confirm this. He went to tour the units. Now whether this is related to the documents that you mentioned, this is not something that I can tell you. I cannot draw such conclusions. It is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have a number of documents that we have placed into e-court regarding the operation of the chain of command in 1998 and 1999, showing numerous instances of General Pavkovic operating within the chain of command. I am not going to go through those documents one at a time for that purpose, but at an appropriate point - whether that be within the next day or so or in the Defence case - we will offer those for admission from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I gather that Mr. Hannis has been prepared to consider whether documents from the Defence should be admitted at this stage in what would normally be an exceptional move. You've heard it happen in the case of Mr. Visnjic, subject to clarification of these documents. If you direct Mr. Hannis to the documents in question, no doubt he'll be able to tell us whether he objects or not before we conclude the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, General, I want to go to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going into a completely different area; and even though it's five minutes early, it might make sense to break now rather than interrupt right after we start. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The trouble is that there are reasons beyond --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are reasons applying to the personnel in the court here that make it much more convenient to stick --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- if we can to the schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, this has been discussed with you at least peripherally, yesterday. I want to go into it just a bit. I think you indicated in your statement and maybe in some of your testimony that you were trained as an infantry officer and that you were an infantry officer for many years in the VJ.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And certainly one thing that you're very familiar with is the -- the problem of friendly fire and making sure that units are deployed in such a way to avoid friendly fire so that your units aren't shooting at each other; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in any combat situation where you are trying to deploy forces that are under different commands, it's important that there be coordination and cooperation; not only for the success of the operation, but to avoid exactly that thing, the friendly fire that we talked about?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, as you've suggested, that there are -- there are basically two ways that this can be accomplished. One, you can create a unified command so that everyone is operating under one single command; or you can create a joint coordinating body of some kind so that before the operation takes place there is cooperation and coordination so that everyone knows what task they have and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the organisation of cooperation -- coordination, there is no need to have such a body. The commander organising the combat activities in fact decides who is supposed to act in concert with whom and coordinate with whom, and he tasks these subordinate units to get in touch with the adjacent units, not necessarily a MUP unit but perhaps an adjacent unit from the same brigade or corps, depending on who is the adjacent unit, to decide on coordination. Lest there should be any instances of friendly fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And if a MUP unit, for instance, is going to undertake an action and requests support from the VJ, then it could be quite helpful to have a meeting to make sure that's properly coordinated; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No meeting is required. The parties that received the order to coordinate with each other in the field must get in touch with each other directly, and then they agree on the axis, the lines of fire, the safety zone in front of the units. This is something that is decided right there on the front line, and this is something that is regulated in an order. But if we're talking about larger-scale operation, then the coordination for all these forces, unless there is a single command, then all these activities must be agreed. So if we're talking about a broader coordination for the use of forces, but as for the coordination of the forces on the front line, this is something that the commanders who are there, commanders of those units, decide because they are best acquainted with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely. No doubt about that, and I actually was referring to the larger operation that you mentioned in your answer. And you talk about it in paragraph 46 of your statement, where you say this: "Although the MUP was not practically subordinated to the army in Kosovo, the two groups were coordinated. The Joint Command compensated for the absence of official subordination by ensuring that coordination for joint operations occurred. In effect, the Joint Command effected de facto coordination and cooperation between the two bodies." Now, that's exactly what we were just talking about, that if you don't have a unified command, then you certainly need some kind of coordination along the lines of what was called a Joint Command at that point; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have explained this earlier, but let me stress this once again. If we're talking about the command, that's one thing. You cannot have two commands. There must be one superior command issuing orders that must be complied with. But if we're talking about coordination, usually these are -- these would be some inter-ministerial staffs and there is no command relationship if you have a coordination. They agree on what should be done, and then each party issues its own commands to its subordinates. So the question about this Joint Command was whether this was a body in charge of coordination or the command issuing orders. I gave you my assessment based on the meeting that I attended, and I cannot go any further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And now we're there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. We'll break again, Mr. Vasiljevic, resume in half an hour. If you could leave the courtroom, please, with the usher. [The witness stands down].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we'll sit again at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I asked Mr. Ackerman to give me three minutes of his time because I wish to tell you the numbers. 3D494, 3D485, and 3D484. These are collegia of the Chief of the General Staff from the same collection disclosed to the Prosecution. In our view, these collegium documents should be tendered into evidence in order to provide the Chamber with a fuller picture of the ways in which the General Staff thought and worked in the relevant period in March 1999 on the one hand. On the other hand we also tried to get from the Government of Yugoslavia, now Serbia, the audio versions of these collegium meetings; but, like the Office of the Prosecutor, we were not successful, which once indicates that there is equality of arms here. If we do manage to get the audio materials, we will of course inform Your Honours. But according to my information which I received from my client, in general, these minutes do reflect what actually happened without going into details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no objection to that based on the way we received them and their offering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll allow these documents to be exhibited as part of the cross-examination material for the third accused. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, we're going to need to backtrack just a little bit, because during the break I found a document I couldn't find while we were talking. And so I'll ask that you take a look at a document, 4D95, please. And this goes to the issue that we were talking about this morning, starting with the directive from General Perisic all the way down through his visit on the 10th of August, 1999. And this is a document 7 August -- I mean -- of 1998. This is a document of 7 August of 1998; and to put it in context, that's a document that would have been one day after the Samardzic order that talked about implementation of 6 August 1998 -- and Mr. Hannis is on his feet?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt my colleague, Your Honour, but 4D95 is not one I received on the e-mail list of documents that was going to be used in cross-examination. I don't have a copy of it, so I don't know what it is. I don't know if there was a subsequent e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis is absolutely correct. It came up during the questioning of this witness today. He said there should be an implementation order if this was something more than plans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think this is an exceptional state of -- set of circumstances, Mr. Hannis, that would justify reference to a document. It's now on the screen. If it causes any particular difficulty for you, obviously, we'll be cognizant of that in deciding what to do ultimately. But it does seem to fit the pattern on the face of it and is worth exploring in our opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have an objection in that regard, Your Honour. I may request to do something similar in re-direct. I just didn't have a copy of it. Now I see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, this is an order issued by General Samardzic on the 7th of August of 1998, and it has to do with the deployment of Yugoslav army units. And I'm mostly interested in paragraphs 1 and 2, and especially 2 where he says: "Pursuant to the approved decision and to support MUP forces, engage army units from the deployment sector which are located behind the combat deployment of the MUP forces by direct fire on individual targets with weapons of the armoured mechanised units, artillery, others, and so forth." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Item number 2, that is, is highlighted, so I cannot really see the letters very clearly. But, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So General Samardzic is actually issuing an order now to the Pristina Corps ordering the implementation of the VJ, as set out initially in that directive that came from General Perisic in July?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the preamble of this order, I don't see any reference to that directive. It describes the situation in Kosovo and then issues an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's true. The language there that I think maybe applies is "pursuant to the approved decision." The other thing you'll notice, if you look at the last page, is that a copy of this was delivered to the Chief of the General Staff, wasn't it?
