utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. It should say it right down there at the bottom. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, I appreciate this is not an order by Perisic; nevertheless, does it in the highlighted part do exactly what you would say Perisic considered should be done only if a state of emergency had been declared; namely, deploy the VJ in support of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a rule, the MUP was the main exponent of the battle against terrorist groups in Kosovo. A decision was reached to secure the state border in a wider belt and the deployment of the forces of the Army of Yugoslavia which can be used to protect facilities. Evidently, at some level, agreement had been reached here for the army to support the MUP forces, which were the main units, the basic units. But there are no elements here to refer to the directive because it isn't mentioned anywhere. What other decisions may have preceded this, I don't know. As I'm expected to confirm the authenticity of these documents, what strikes me here is that I don't see the usual stamps here, the seals, showing that this was actually sent and registered in the relevant command. If this was sent by the commander of the army, Dusan Samardzic, to the Pristina Corps or some other corps, it would have to say that it was sent and whether it was coded or not and so on, or there should be a stamp from the Pristina Corps confirming the receipt of the document. On more than one of these documents, I have not seen the square stamp that would confirm receipt of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now I wonder if you could deal with the question I actually asked you. Does the order purport in the highlighted part to do exactly what you would say Perisic considered should be done only if a state of emergency had been declared? Or does it do something different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If a state of emergency is declared, not a state of war, then this could refer to a stage that had been planned. But in the preamble to this order there is no reference to the directive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. Just let's forget that for the moment. Look at the exact terms of the highlighted paragraph, not the one on the screen. Go back to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, the front page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I understood that Perisic's position was that certain things could only be done if a state of emergency had been declared. Have I got that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I understood one of these things was deploying the VJ in support of the MUP. Have I got that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not as a separate support task. The army was deployed in the broader Kosovo area to maintain control over the area and to provide support to the MUP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... More specifically. To deploy an armoured brigade of the VJ in support of the MUP. That would require a state of emergency. Was that his opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was, yes. Such a large unit, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, is that not exactly what this highlighted paragraph says was to be done, that the VJ armoured mechanised units and artillery were to be used in support of MUP action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've answered my question. That's all I want to know at the moment. I understand what you're saying about the lack of reference back to the directive and the lack of a link, but we can move on to other matters now. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And now I'm going back to the area I was pursuing before the break. I'd like you to look at 4D91. This is a -- an order of the 3rd Army command of 30 July 1998 from General Samardzic of the 3rd Army. You'll notice at the beginning, it says it's: "Pursuant to the order of the Chief of the General Staff." It indicates that General Samardzic has set up a 3rd Army forward command post in Pristina, that any decisions concerning the engagement of army forces in Kosovo and Metohija are to be made by the army Chief of Staff, that would be the 3rd Army Chief of Staff, in line with decisions of Samardzic; and then he, in paragraph 3, appears to exercise a great deal of control over the commander of the Pristina Corps and what he is authorised to do. And it says this, that the commander of the Pristina Corps - which at that time was General Pavkovic - was to attend all the meetings of this body called the Joint Command. But prior to going to those meetings, he needed to tell the army Chief of Staff what requests he knew would be made at those meetings and to get the permission of the army Chief of Staff to agree to those requests; and then after the meeting, he was to report back to the Chief of Staff on what was accepted at the Joint Command meeting and whether there were any other requests made and then seek permission with regard to those requests. And he was then to inform the Joint Command of any decisions made by Samardzic with regard to the appropriate use of the army. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Very precisely developed the place and the role of the then-commander of the Pristina Corps in the work of the body called the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right. And the other thing I suggest to you that's significant here is that there was this forward command post of the 3rd Army operating right there, in Pristina, with apparently the army Chief of Staff being right there in Pristina so that General Pavkovic was not permitted to make any use of the VJ without getting the complete approval of the Chief of Staff through General Samardzic. That necessarily follows, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the other thing that I think is clear if -- from this order, if you agree with me. General Samardzic was maintaining complete control of the operation of the Pristina Corps, as he should have. And he was treating anything going on within that Joint Command as requests as to which he was the final decision-maker as to whether the army would be used in accordance with those requests?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if we look then at Exhibit 4D94.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is another one that I don't have on my list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 4D94 was sent to them a long time ago, I think, Your Honour. I was told that it was by my staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have the e-mail from the 19th, and it doesn't appear to be listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's see what it is, Mr. Hannis, and then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's apparently not available on e-court, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, as my colleague, Mr. Sepenuk, once said, heads will roll.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to something else and see if the situation changes in the interim.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can always make use of it at a later date, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to leave this area now and go to the meetings that went on in Belgrade where General Ojdanic had asked General Pavkovic to come to Belgrade and meet with he and then also Milosevic regarding a report that certain crimes were being committed in the course of what was going on in Kosovo. And I just want to direct your attention to that. One of the things that General Pavkovic explained in the meeting on the 16th was that he'd seen Skorpions and Boca in Prolom Banja wearing NATO-type uniforms. And I think you simply made the comment in your testimony that you didn't know what General Pavkovic was doing in Prolom Banja. And I suspect that's because you didn't know that there was a 3rd Army reserve command post there in Prolom Banja, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, there being a 3rd Army reserve command post there, it was totally appropriate for the 3rd Army commander to visit there, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it was at this meeting on the 16th that you heard for the first time the recommendation of General Pavkovic that he wanted to form a Joint Commission to establish responsibility for crimes and that he made that recommendation to Ojdanic in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The first time I heard about the initiative to establish this commission was from Lieutenant-Colonel Djurovic on the 9th of May when he set out certain problems in general in Kosovo. On the 16th General Pavkovic officially declared his standpoint, but I knew indirectly about this on the 9th of July -- sorry, I apologise, not the 9th of July, I meant to say the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. And the recommendation was then repeated by General Pavkovic in the meeting with Milosevic on the 17th, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, after these meetings, you made a trip to Kosovo between the 1st and 9th of June of 1999, and the purpose of that trip was to conduct a fact-finding mission, among other things, regarding the commission of crimes following the revelations that went -- took place in these meetings in Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it was not until the 9th of July [as interpreted], but the 7th. On the 7th, in the morning, we were already on our way back passing through Kosovo on our way to Nis. So I was there from the 1st to the 7th. The rest is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. My question about --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. For the record, I should indicate that that should probably read the 7th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's 7th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] June, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, your meeting with Milosevic was on the 17th of May where these matters were first discussed with Milosevic. My question is: Why did you wait from the 17th of May until the 1st of June to pursue this mission, this fact-finding mission? What was the cause for the delay? There was about a two-week hiatus there.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, when General Gajic and I set out, there was a rebellion in a unit at Kosovo which left its positions and arrived in Krusevac. Our task was to find the organisers of the rebellion and to assist on the ground to have the unit returned to Kosovo with weapons, because they had abandoned their positions with their weapons. So we were in Krusevac from the time we set out to Kosovo until the 7th. Colonel Antic was with us at Krusevac. He was the chief of security in the 3rd Army and he was there with us on the same task.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I've managed to confuse myself with that question. Either I don't understand your answer or you didn't answer my question. What I was trying to find out is why you didn't -- you waited until the 1st of June to go to Kosovo when these revelations happened on the 16th/17th of May, in that area. I mean, why the delay between 17 May and 1st of June? Did you answer that? Is that what you told me just now? And if you did, just say yes, and I'll try and understand it.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, during your testimony, Mr. Hannis - and I think it was at page 17 of the rough version of the transcript - Mr. Hannis was asking you if in this fact-finding trip you had gathered up any information about any of the locations mentioned in the indictment, and he named several of those locations. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. When did I learn about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you went to Kosovo on your fact-finding mission, Mr. Hannis was asking you yesterday at page 17 about various locations in Kosovo where the Prosecution contends that crimes were committed, asking you if you received any information about any of those locations. And you had indicated that you hadn't; and then he asked you if there were any security officers stationed in any of those locations. Do you remember that line of questioning and your answers?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do. I thought you were referring to some other period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, it's that period. Now, just for an example, if there were allegations that crimes were committed in, let's say Suva Reka, whether or not the security service would have knowledge of that wouldn't depend at all on whether the security service had someone stationed in Suva Reka. It would depend on whether the security officer associated with the units involved in that operation was aware that crimes were committed there and had reported them, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your investigation, as you told the Judges yesterday, involved checking with all of the brigades there down to the battalion level for whatever information was available through the security officers in those organisations?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not say all of the brigades but a certain number of brigades and some independent battalions; not all the brigades that were part of either the Pristina Corps and least of all of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the transcript here in front of me, but it will show what it shows. If -- if it's true that crimes were committed in a certain location and that there was no report from a security officer regarding those crimes, then I suspect that a couple of things are true. One would be that it's not true that those crimes were committed; another would be that there was no VJ unit involved and, therefore, a security officer for that unit would not be aware. Those are a couple of possibilities; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, can you ask a direct question. I don't know what you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what I'm asking you is more in the nature of argument anyhow, and I'll just drop it. Now, on 1 June 1999, that was when you attended this meeting that you were told was a meeting of the Joint Command; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And at that meeting, General Lukic made some kind of a report, General Lazarevic made some kind of report, Pavkovic then made some kind of report; but you said at the very end Sainovic then said: "Okay, do as you've planned." What was it in your view that was planned?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite specific, what was planned was the action in Drenica and in Trpeza where the plan was to engage 300 police officers. So this was an action that was to take place the next day. And in addition to what he said, "Do it as planned," Mr. Sainovic added that in the next three or four days the anti-terrorist operation should be completed; in other words, all those groups should be crushed and destroyed. And the second thing that he said - and that was based on what General Pavkovic said - that more attention should be paid to organising the activities in a better way and to improve the cooperation between the MUP and the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So this operation was -- did not involve any support from the VJ, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not note this down, and this is not something that stuck in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And nothing came out of that meeting that would be interpreted by you as any kind of a classic order of command, an order to carry out a certain activity. It simply looked like a meeting of information and coordination, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now this is a terminology issue, but, obviously, there was a meeting where the proposals that were made were verified. The order -- no order was written - this is what I said - and I don't know whether General Pavkovic actually complied with the things that were specified as early as in July, which would be the obligation of an officer attending a meeting of such a Joint Command. Whether he informed the General Staff, whether he got his approval for what the army was supposed to do, I don't know about that. I only told you of what I learned during my brief stay there and with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you've answered my question by telling me a lot of things you don't know, and that's fine. You have no knowledge of any -- any combat reports, documents in the nature of combat reports, being made to this alleged Joint Command or any orders coming down from the Chief of the General Staff to this Joint Command? In other words, this Joint Command wasn't within the chain of command of the Yugoslav Army, was it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you my answer. I saw the combat reports and the combat documents only when they were shown to me here. At the time when I was in Kosovo and while I was in active service, I did not see them. Now, I cannot really make conclusions whether this was part of the chain of command or not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise; we didn't catch the last part of the answer because of the paper shuffling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we've now solved the mystery of 4D94. It apparently is 4D125. And I would like to go into that just very briefly, and I think that one was notified to Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do have that one, but I would like to try and clear up the rest of the General's answer that the interpreters said they weren't able to hear because of shuffling papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I missed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you give us again, Mr. Vasiljevic, the very end of your last answer. You said that you could not really make conclusions whether this was part of the chain of command or not. Did you say something about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now you should have in front of you 4D125, which is the document I was trying to show you earlier. And this one is dated the 1st of August of 1998, and I'm interested in this document for what it says with regard to the Joint Command. Do you have it in front of you? This is a Samardzic order to the Pristina Corps, also to the forward command post of the 3rd Army. And what this says that -- in the preamble, it indicates that there was a Joint Command request for engagement of Pristina Corps units in what's called the third phase of the operation to be carried out on the 2nd of August. And General Samardzic says in paragraph 1 of his order that he forbids the use of Pristina Corps units with reinforcements, as requested by the Joint Command, until such time as some kind of appropriate approval is issued from a higher level. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. My name is Mihajlo Bakrac, and I am one of the lawyers representing Mr. Lazarevic. I have some questions lined up for you, but I have another extra question proceeding from your answer. When Mr. Ackerman asked you whether you had seen any combat reports sent to the Joint Command or an order sent to the Joint Command, you said that you had seen combat documents and reports when they were shown to you. What kind of combat reports and combat documents are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combat report by the commander of the Pristina Corps or some other unit, so two such reports were shown to me by Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, but not addressed to the Joint Command. I just wanted to clarify things for the record. So you did not see any such documents addressed to the Joint Command, because the transcript reflects that you did see such documents here?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not addressed to the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Now I will move on to the questions that I had prepared. And perhaps I can ask you a question that again proceeds from the cross-examination, the previous cross-examination. At issue was when a combat activity is carried out a combat action and when the Army of Yugoslavia executes coordination with the MUP forces, you said that this coordination between the adjacent units is something that is organised in the field directly?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that this is something that is regulated in a document or a combat report -- a combat order, and then it is implemented in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In the field, you will agree with me, General, that there should be a communications system in place between the adjacent units?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm telling you this because you were shown a Prosecution exhibit, P1052 on the radio communications and radio stations plan. And as far as I understand, you answered that this was the usual way to set up the communications and that there should have been communications set up between adjacent units.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This plan does not contain just the -- does not refer only to adjacent units, but to the superior station. But this is something -- this is something -- this is the system that is used for communication between adjacent units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Let me go back to paragraph 10 of your statement. And, in my opinion, it is my impression that this paragraph is -- has not been fully elaborated, and I would like to ask you to clarify some things here. So what you say here -- you talk about the people who were sitting on the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and you said that the strategic groups, 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Army were subordinate to the General Staff, and you mentioned the commanders of these three armies and the commander of the air force and of the navy. What I want to know, first of all, is how many corps were there in those strategic groups?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 3rd Army there were two corps, the Nis Corps and the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: As for the 1st and the 2nd Army, they also had their own corps?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How many of them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, two or three corps -- I have to apologise. So you agree that there was the anti-aircraft defence corps that covered the entire territory of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that there was the air force corps that also covered the whole of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So there would be a total of about ten corps?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that the establishment post of the corps commander is either a general-major or a colonel-general?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A general-major.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And the Chief of Staff would be colonel?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that in 1999 the number of establishment posts in the Yugoslav Army for generals was more than 120 such posts?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You will agree that in 1999 the number of establishment posts for generals in the VJ was 120 or even more than that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't have the exact figure; but if we compare that to the number of generals in the JNA, I don't think there were that many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But there were many of them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The reason why I'm asking you this is because I found it strange that after you enumerated the commanders of the armies and of the corps, that you said that the Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army, General Stojimirovic; the commander of the Pristina Corps, General Lazarevic; and Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps, Colonel Stevanovic were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Defence counsel please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question has not been completed because you're both speaking too quickly. We need a gap between the question and answer to allow the interpreter to catch up. So we didn't get the question, Mr. Bakrac, and you need to ask it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I do have to apologise. I will try to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So, General, I ask these questions. I'm not contesting the fact that this perhaps does not follow from the examination, but I find it strange that after you enumerate all the corps and all the corps commanders and all the generals, the Chief of Staff, saying that this was a lieutenant-colonel according to the formation -- to the establishment; and then what you do, you go on to list, in addition to the three generals that are army commanders and the generals in the General Staff, you mention three other people as key persons in the Yugoslav Army. Can you please answer, why is this so?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not asked to list all the key generals and all the key people in the Yugoslav Army and all the arms of the army. I was asked quite specifically for the command staff in the 3rd Army and in the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The reason why I ask you is because above the words that are above those three names is "other key VJ personnel were," and that's why I thought that this must be a mistake of some sort. So this relates only to the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not the key people in the Army of Yugoslavia, because I could give you a number of other generals who -- whose rating was the same or even higher than theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Surely the way to read this is that these are key personnel in relation to the indictment, so that we know who's who in relation to things that matter in this case. Thank goodness, for once, the investigator seems to have been concentrating on establishing things confined to the circumstances of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I thought that there was a need to clarify this, since -- given the context in which this is presented. But let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, again, for the purpose of clarification, you list here that Colonel Stevanovic was the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps. I would like to ask you to think back because my information is different, and would you agree with me that the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps - we're talking about 1999 - was, in fact, General Veroljub Zivkovic, rather than Colonel Stevanovic, and that Colonel Stevanovic was in fact the operations officer in the corps?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I cannot dispute that because I was not a member of the Pristina Corps. It must be as General Lazarevic stated. If he provided that information, then it must be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I feel an obligation to explain to you. It is important for us to clarify these things because of our Defence case which we are to present later. I want to remove any doubt or discrepancies as for certain people who may or may not appear here in the courtroom. Let us move on. General, sir, I wanted to know whether it is true that in Kosovo, in addition to the Pristina Corps, in 1999 during war there were also some units of the military district; then the 202nd Rear Logistics Base, which was not subordinated to the Pristina Corps; then some units of the air force and anti-aircraft defence units, which were not commanded by the Pristina Corps but by the anti-aircraft defence and air force; as well as some civilian protection units commanded by the Ministry of Defence. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were not an integral part of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've mentioned this, and I wanted to ask you whether it is correct that in 1999 and as early as 1998, as was shown to you by Mr. Ackerman, at the command post, or rather, in Pristina there was a forward command post of the 3rd Army. And it also testifies that there was no breach in the chain of command between the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army since there was a forward command post of the 3rd Army there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was in the period referenced to by the -- or in the document when the forward command post of the 3rd Army was in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm asking you. Did you know that in 1998 and 1999, throughout the war, there was a forward command post of the 3rd Army in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I suppose. I was at that post during the meeting on the 1st of June, but no one told me that and I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will make a short break to re-organise myself, but I will try to spend as little time as possible for my colleagues who will follow. In paragraph 52, General, you mention that. I wanted to know this: Was there an obligation in place on the part of the security organs within the Pristina Corps to report alleged crimes to General Lazarevic, him being the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And then General Lazarevic would forward that information up to the 3rd Army via the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he was in possession of such information, he was supposed to forward them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that as regards potential crimes, there was three lines of reporting: The first one was from the corps commander to the 3rd Army commander; then another one by the security service, or rather, within its structure?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Between the security organs of the corps and the army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And as the third concerned the military judicial organs?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, is it also true that - and we saw an order presented by Mr. Visnjic - that as of the beginning of the war, there was a war military prosecutor's office for the Pristina Corps as well as a military -- war military court of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that within the Pristina district there was also a war military prosecutor's office and military court of the Pristina district, separate from the aforementioned ones?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we discussed reporting and notification. I don't have sufficient time on my hands to pursue that further and I don't wish to present some or parts of our Defence case, but you mentioned information you received from the deputy of the security chief of the Pristina Corps and the information you received in early May. My learned friend Mr. Ackerman showed us a report from mid-June -- mid-April, and I just wanted to comment or wanted you to comment on a Defence exhibit, 5D84.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that could be brought up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, do you wish to acquaint yourself with the document first? It has three pages. I wanted to draw your attention to what I'm interested in. In the heading we can see that this was a Pristina Corps command document with a number and the date of the 3rd of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It was sent to the 3rd Army command and its operation centre; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It is a combat report, and in its item 1, it states "Enemy." Item 2: "Situation in units and activities."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Item 3 is the "Manning strength." Item 4: "Morale." Item 5: "Security situation." In the last line of item 5, "Security situation," it reads: "During the preceding days, 32 criminal reports were submitted against the perpetrators for crimes; eight for murder, one for rape, three for attempted murder, two for taking vehicles, six for theft, and 12 for absence without official leave." Item 6 is "Command and communications situation."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And item 7: "Logistics support."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go to the last page, please. I believe the next page is the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the last page - and it is important because of the signature and so that you saw the entire document - can you tell me whether this is an exemplary type of combat report the way it is supposed to be drafted? Is there anything missing, in view of the Rules of Service and the regulations in place concerning the drafting of such documents?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this is in keeping with a classic example of the combat report, treating with the main issues, depending on the type of activities and command organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Today you were shown a combat report, and you had a remark when you stated that types of offences were not to be stated. However, we see them listed here. Is it correct that in a combat report it would be quite ordinary to have it summed up like this and broken down into various offences, particularly having in mind that there was another chain of reporting within the military judicial organs which would go into much greater detail?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the individual cases mentioned here, if they are a typical example of the situation, then a separate report could be drafted. The organ who provided that data could draft a separate report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, I wanted to show you one last document. It is a combat report on the next day. I wanted to have your comment, since it is different in form.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 5D85 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you will agree with me, I presume, that this is another Pristina Corps command document from the next day, this being the 4th of April, 1999, sent also to the 3rd Army command and its operations centre. However, we see that its form is different. The items are the same, but this document was a Telefax message.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only have the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 1. We have enemy electronic activity or operations. Could we please go to page 2 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We also have security situation, and in the last line it also reads: "During the previous day there were six criminal reports submitted against alleged perpetrators, against two privates, three VO, and one VPU."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it in English, but I see the stamp there by the teleprinting station which has sent this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So this way of sending out combat reports was in place, and it included everything that was supposed to be in a combat report?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. During your examination-in-chief, when examined by my learned friend, Mr. Hannis, you said that there were two types of offences within the army; one of which could be sanction by disciplinary measures and the other one would be treated as a criminal matter?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: For disciplinary measures to be imposed, the commander was in charge of those?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could put it even in a better way. The chain of command was tasked with issuing disciplinary measures. It can be within the purview of the commander if it is a milder disciplinary breach that went against the regulations. If it was a graver offence without any element of the criminal -- of a criminal offence, then it was treated by disciplinary courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I just wanted to hear this. For infractions, for minor infractions, they could be sanctioned by the commander. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were acts which would not result in negative consequences for the unit in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: An example, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Say two recruits left the barracks without official leave, got drunk in a nearby village without any incident, they simply returned drunk, then it was within the purview of the commander. But if they also committed a theft in the course of that, if it was a minor theft, it could also be dealt with by the commander. But if it was an aggravated theft or robbery, then it would follow a different procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I have to pause for interpreters. General, for more serious offences, there were disciplinary courts in place. Would you agree with me if I said that during the war there was a military disciplinary court in Nis?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in existence in peacetime as well as during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. For criminal offences treated by the military court, it wasn't within the purview of the commander. His only obligation was to submit a criminal report to the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't his only obligation, or rather, it wasn't an obligation on his part only. He wasn't the only one who was to report on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, inter alia, it was the commander as well as the security organs. They would submit a report, and then the courts would try and deal with the case.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Having all this in mind and within the context of the previously mentioned two combat reports, can we say in that specific example General Lazarevic, having learned of certain criminal offences, did all he could to report that to the command and submit a criminal report. Beyond that, were there any other obligations on his part?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That concluded his obligations. Based on the information which would be provided in general terms, say a murder was committed, then the army command was supposed to ask for a detailed report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And it was standard procedure?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say it was standard procedure, but there was such a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Still on the same topic. Do you know, General, that over 40 professional members of the army were disciplined by the military disciplinary court; over 30 officers were removed from duty, including two brigade commanders, two Chiefs of Staff, 12 security organs, and 12 battalion commanders?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have knowledge of that -- this complete picture, but I did know about some individual cases. I think that these instances, where officers were replaced, I think it was in the 125th Brigade, and I know that some officers were replaced because they did not perform their tasks properly. But this is just an illustration of the general situation. I did not -- I was not aware of this -- these total figures that you just gave me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Do you know that the military prosecutor's office and the military court at the Pristina Corps sent weekly reports to the Pristina military corps and to the 3rd Army and to the General Staff about all the cases that were prosecuted before them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have specific information to that effect that this was done every seven days, but I do know that there was this general provision that they had to report up the chain of command but I don't know how it was actually done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did the Ministry of the Interior send information to the military security service, information about any improper conduct by the VJ personnel? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak about the highest level, so we're talking about the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia and the security administration. We had problems constantly, and this is something that was discussed at the 17th of May meeting. It was stated that there was insufficient cooperation between the MUP and the army and that there was no regular reporting. But as far as I know, no reports actually pertained to the events in Kosovo -- I mean the crimes or any other criminal offences. But a report was made but not to the security administration but to President Milosevic about Jugoslav Petrusic's stay in Kosovo with his volunteers. But those were exceptional reports that we received from them at that level. I couldn't tell you anything about how this cooperation proceeded at lower levels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Is your answer to that question that the Ministry of the Interior did not send information to the military security service about improper conduct by VJ personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you said that as far as Colonel Djurovic, deputy Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps, that you spoke with him. Did you get any information from him that the corps command, whenever it learned that there was some suspicion, that no measures were taken; in other words, that there was a suspicion that a VJ soldier was involved in some criminal activities, that it -- that the corps command did not take any efforts to investigate that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djurovic did not complain to me about that, and he did not complain about what the corps commander did with the intelligence obtained by the security organs; and as regards this initiative to form a commission to head up those investigations, he was actually involved in those investigations. So Djurovic did not have any complaints about his commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, that was to be my next question. You have information that the initiative to establish such a commission was actually launched by the corps command and the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say that with that certainty. I know that he was involved in the setting up of this commission. Now, whether -- as to who ordered the commission to be set up, General Pavkovic or General Lazarevic, but they were both involved in its work anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do you know that General Lazarevic, as the corps commander, when he received a report from the military judicial organs about measures that had been taken against the persons who perpetrated crimes, he then took this report containing the name of the perpetrator, the criminal offence, and the sanction that was imposed, he sent it down the chain of command to the subordinate units in order to prevent -- deter any further crimes. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that because I didn't go into such details. That would be something that the organs for the morale would have to do, because they have to take preventive measures and to take measures to maintain morale. But I do believe that this kind of report would be sent from one morale organ to the other, but not from one security organ to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I was late entering a document into e-court, so I will deal with this in the Defence case. I merely wanted to check whether you had any knowledge of that. What I also want to know, General, is whether you know that the commander of the Pristina Corps, General Lazarevic, from the 12th of April, 1999, sent combat reports daily in addition to the operations centre of the 3rd Army to the operations centre of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to ask my colleague Mr. Hannis to assist me. I have a question related to paragraph 57. It's been redacted, but I don't want to mention the persons listed there, just the location. I don't know if there's any need for us to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you referring to paragraph 58?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 57 was not redacted, was it? Oh, it is. There is a redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There is a redacted version, Your Honour. I didn't ask him any questions about this paragraph, but it is redacted in the publicly filed version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall go into private session to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 62 you spoke about the crime in Izbica. Do you know that because the army was not actually present in that area, that the exhumation and all the investigative measures were ordered by the district court in Kosovska Mitrovica and that the exhumation proceedings and the investigation into the crime was conducted by the district court in Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who had the subject matter or territorial jurisdiction over that case. I merely mentioned that I knew that an exhumation would be carried out and that the autopsies would be carried out in the Kosovska Mitrovica hospital, and I did -- I said that I did not know which organs were in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So we can say that you did not see any attempt to cover up anything that was actually going on as far as the crimes were concerned?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I have just a few short questions. General, is it true that before the 1st of May, so in April in other words, the security organs of the Pristina Corps visited and so did the chief of the security service, General Farkas, and the expert team from the security administration, that they visited the military police in the Pristina Corps and that at that time chief of security, Farkas, proposed that the 1st Battalion of the military police be reinforced, that they receive additional reinforcements?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that General Geza and some other officers, I think they were actually from the military police, that they went to Pristina. I think it was for the 1st of May holidays, because I was in Montenegro at the time. And when I got back from Montenegro, it must have been sometime on the 3rd or 4th of May; then at the daily briefing, General Geza said that he had been in Pristina and I believe that he was there over the 1st of May holidays.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, thank you very much. Is it also true that General Farkas did not notice or file any reports about any failures or omissions in the operation of the military police units in the Pristina Corps following his tour of inspection?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact, what he did is he commended them. He said that they were highly active and highly capable officers. And he said this was, in fact, a pool of personnel to be promoted to other higher posts, and he was very, very -- he said many positive things about their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: For the transcript, we have only the military police listed here, but what you just said also referred to the security organs?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the assessment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only to the security organs of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know that the security organ in the Pristina Corps, in order to improve the cooperation with the military judicial organs in the military district of Pristina and the Pristina Corps, had appointed Captain Nesic as the point man there? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, do you know that the command organs in the military security and military judicial organs, together with three experts and pathologist themes from the military academy -- medical academy, carried out several exhumations at Ribanje, Cikatovo, and another place, although there were no indications that the military personnel were responsible for the commission of these crimes, specifically to prevent any cover-ups of any crimes and to investigate any suspicions of any crimes?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that pathologist teams were involved in exhumations, but I don't have the details that you just presented to me, whether it was in Cikatovo or some other location. But this is based on my stay there. I learned there that exhumations had been carried out as part of the sanitization procedures, and I learned about that at a meeting with General Pavkovic as the Chief of General Staff. I think that the chief of medical corps was also there. He had all the cases there with him where the area had to be sanitized.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may have two or three questions. I don't know whether we should make the break now. You said that we have very stringent rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, for two or three questions, let's see if we can complete your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, I have a question that I thought might be asked because it stems from an examination of a previous witness and also, to a certain extent, from your statement. You spoke about the Fehmi Agani case. Do you know anything about the murder of Bajram Kelmendi?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You have no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then, Your Honour, I don't have the two or three questions I initially thought I would have, so I completed my cross-examination within the time-limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Lunchtime now, Mr. Vasiljevic, so again would you leave with the usher and we'll see you back here in an hour at quarter to 2.00. [The witness stands down].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume then. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Vasiljevic. My name is Dan Ivetic and I represent Mr. Sreten Lukic relative to these proceedings today. I am going to ask you some questions relative to your testimony you have just given and to clarify some points in your written statement to try to better understand things. It is important that you pay close attention to everything I ask you and give as honest and complete answer as possible. In particular if you don't know an answer or if it would be speculation, please let me know that. Now, first of all, in your testimony, yesterday, at page 8951, line 22, you stated you knew General Lukic for a period of time; and, indeed, in your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, you stated several times that you knew General Lukic very well. So, first of all, I would like to ask you to tell the Trial Chamber how long you have known Mr. Sreten Lukic, the man sitting behind me, and under what circumstances you have known him.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I haven't had any extensive contacts with Mr. Lukic. I believe we met during my term of service in Bosnia, although I am not sure. He greeted me at the 1st of June meeting when I came there, rather warmly, too. We would encounter each other on occasion, although I cannot recall the specific instances during our military careers. In short, that's the extent of our relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say during your term of service in Bosnia, are you talking about the time-period when you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the interviews with the Office of the Prosecutor, you also at one point in time referenced that you believed that Mr. Lukic might be affiliated with the RDB, the State Security Sector. Do you recall making those statements?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not that Mr. Lukic; it is another man. This was Gajic. It was simply a wrong name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for clearing that up with me. Now, as far as the time that you say that you met Mr. Lukic in Sarajevo, do you recall whether there were any other persons with you in your encounters with Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said we met in Sarajevo. I said that I know him from the time when I served not in Sarajevo but in all of Bosnia. I don't know exactly when or where we met for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall what position or employment Mr. Lukic had at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether he was serving in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, although I am uncertain.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you -- would your recollection be refreshed if I told you that this gentleman, Sreten Lukic, never served in Bosnia and served his entire career in the MUP in the Republic of Serbia? Would you be surprised by that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be surprised. It is possible, but I don't think it is something of importance to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, what I'm trying to find out is when you talk about General Lukic, is there a possibility that you are mixing up various persons, since, I submit, one of the first times that you met Mr. Lukic was in June of 1999 in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember well meeting him then, and we greeted each other as people that know each other. It is possible that we met on previous occasions in the republican MUP in 1991 or 1992, when I served in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's move on briefly to the -- to your attendance at a meeting in Pristina that you had called -- that you said was called the Joint Command at which there were several police and army officers present. Am I correct that it was your impression at that time that Sreten Lukic of the MUP was effectively the least senior person present at that meeting? I think you called him the last hole on the flute in the interview that you had with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't use such a term, no holes, no flutes. His rank was that of major-general. As far as I knew at the time, he was commander of the MUP forces in Kosovo; that's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that you did not in your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor say that -- that due to the seating position at the table, he was in B/C/S "zadnja rufnja frula" [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember having said that. You should be able to find that in my statement, the exact words I used.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's where I got them. Now, if we can talk about your impression of that meeting, is it correct that there were two other generals from the MUP present and the third, whose name we will not mention since it was -- it's been used in private session, who were either present or supposed to be present at that meeting in addition to General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, according to the information that you had received relative to the meeting, am I correct that members of the RDB, the State Security Service, were usually present for such meetings as well?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were usually present. I didn't attend such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You previously mentioned Mr. Gajic of the RDB. Am I correct that Mr. Gajic was the senior -- was the chief of the RDB in the province of Kosovo and Metohija during most of 1997, 1998, and part of 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't have precise information as to when he came in Kosovo. I know he was there in 1998 and, according to the information I had, in 1999, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And his deputy, who later replaced him in that position, was a gentleman by the name of Mr. Vilotijevic. Do you -- are you familiar with him as well?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last name is familiar. I know that such a person was in the DB.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's move on to some other questions. First of all, sir, am I correct that you never finished any formal course work, either at the police academy or any such similar institution, relating to the operation, the organisation, the command structure, or the functioning of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't complete the police academy. I completed military schools. As for Mr. Lukic, he attended police schools and then he became a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That was my point, that you had not attended police schools, sir. In your training at the military schools, you never had any formal course work relating to the operation, organisation, command structure, or functioning of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for police education, I completed one year for security officers of the JNA and a senior course for security. As I said, I never attended the police academy. Through my contacts with the MUP in peacetime and in the 30 years of practice and working in the military security organs, I often communicated with people from the MUP and I was well-acquainted with their [as interpreted] structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is your knowledge of what schools Sreten Lukic attended based upon your security sources, your security organs?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There's one issue that we need to clear up in the transcript, Your Honours. At page 86, line 5, what is entered into the transcript is "well-acquainted with their structure," and I believe the witness indicated that he is "well-acquainted roughly with the structure." We can ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, is that, in fact, what you said about your -- communicating with people from the MUP, that you are roughly -- that you are roughly -- "well-acquainted with their rough structure?"

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their structure, in general terms, to the extent I needed as a security officer, is what I knew about. It sufficed for me to communicate with them. I presume Mr. Lukic did not have detailed information on the functioning of the military security, on the other hand. Therefore, I would say that the extent which I was acquainted with the MUP structure was the same as his extent of being acquainted with the military structure, although I am inclined to believe that I was more acquainted with their structure to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to -- with respect to the public security division of the Serbian MUP, am I correct that your activities at the army's security administration did not cause you to have regular, collaborative work with this service of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean "regular, collaborative work." We collaborated with the Serbian MUP on issues which were of interest to both parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you -- when you say you collaborated with the Serbian MUP on issues that were of interest to both parties, isn't it true that you are referring to the RDB portion of the MUP, since they had a similar modus operandi, similar essence, in terms of what their jurisdiction was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have that separated in my mind as for the cooperation with the SDB, when it concerned state security and then I cooperated with the RDB, and such contacts continued until 1992 when I was retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You've mentioned the SDB and you've mentioned the RDB. My original question for you was with respect to the RJB, the Reso Javni Bedbestni [phoen] of the MUP, the public sector or division. Am I correct that your work at the UB or KOS did not include regular collaboration with the RJB?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said it was incorrect. It is separate, the SDB, and what later became the RDB. And I know quite clearly what the public security sector is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What type of work, collaborative work, did you undertake through your agency with the public security sector, the RJB?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can talk about the period between 1990 and 1992 because that is of interest to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is not. I was trying to establish what knowledge you have pertaining to the period of 1998 to 1999, but I'll move on. Now, as far as the state security division of the Serbian MUP is concerned, the RDB, am I correct that your former agency, the military security administration, with the acronym KOS or UB, that your agency and the RDB were largely involved in rivalry with one another and even some in-fighting and animosity practically since the old SFRY UDBA security organ was disbanded and broken up at the fourth plenary of the SFRY, as you stated in your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no mutual animosity, as you say. However, there was a sort of special relationship between their personnel after the fourth plenary in 1964. At that time, the popular opinion was that they were controlled by the military security, which is incorrect. When I was arrested in 1992, some people from the state security said, "Well, serves them right. This is paying back for what happened to us in 1964." I'm talking about it in very broad terms, not necessarily about the situation as it really was. There were people who had real issues with the fourth plenary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During the time-period prior to your premature retirement and arrest, did you have any -- did you personally have any conflicts with the RDB institution or senior officials within that institution such as Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Simatovic, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was no conflict. I gave an example from that period, late April 1992 or thereabouts if I'm not mistaken, I think it was the 22nd or the 23rd of April, because the RDB or the State Security Service of Serbia, as it was that time, arrested retired Colonel Milan Damjanovic, who had real operational jurisdiction -- or who was under the operational jurisdiction of the security administration without consulting the security administration and without even notifying us. So this was the only conflict that I presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that you suspected the RDB had a role in both your forced retirement and the false rumours about your loyalty and that of your Macedonian deputy as well as your subsequent arrest. Isn't that what you told the Office of the Prosecutor in your interview with them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please be specific in your question, you -- your question required a lengthy explanation. Could you please tell me what the actual question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you suspect that the RDB had a role in your forced retirement from the security administration and/or your subsequent arrest?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's was something that I suspect. I have facts to that effect, but if I am at liberty to make comments about that I will do so. You're now trying to establish a link between the events in 1992 and my purported aversion towards them which is completely spurious. I did not have any animosity either towards the MUP or the RDB.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you had any knowledge or suspicion that the RDB had a role in your forced retirement or forced arrest. I believe you can answer that with a yes or no without going into details from 1992, which is not that relevant to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was the arrest not in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The arrest was in 1992, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So has he not answered the question by saying that he has facts to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's not how the translation came in through me, but let me just check. Oh, okay, that has answered that. I apologised then. I must have missed something in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if I can clarify something. The other day, yesterday, actually, you testified, it was page 57 of the un-updated transcript, lines 3 through 17, that the state security division, the RDB, was independent of the other sector of the MUP and directly linked to Milosevic rather than to the Minister of the Interior. At page 55 of the transcript, you also stated that General Stevanovic, even as assistant minister of the interior, was not in charge of the state security division nor to superior Rade Markovic. Now, my question is as follows: Is it your understanding that an officer of the RJB or public security division, such as General Stevanovic, could not command over Rade Markovic or the RDB?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He could not have commanded over Rade Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would that answer be the same for all the generals, colonels, et cetera, of the RJB, the public security division; that is to say, that they could not command over the RDB or RDB officials, such as Rade Markovic, David Gajic, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a matter of principle. These were two completely independent divisions, and the Minister of the Interior was their superior, I mean the Serbian Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could focus to try and see a little bit to your knowledge of the RJB on the public security side of the MUP. Do you know how many bureaus or "Upravas" there were on the RJB side each with an executive officer or "nacelnik"?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, and I did not make any statements to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move on now just briefly to -- to clarify some geographic points relating to your encounter, the unfortunate encounter, with the JSO at Trstenik. First of all, am I correct that -- strike that. How far away is Trstenik from the province of Kosovo-Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean as the crow flies or if you go by the road?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you know both, both would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be very accurate; I would need a map. But as the crow flies, that should be around 150 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, which -- where are we in the written statement now?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We're at the Trstenik incident which he testified about yesterday and which is at the -- at paragraphs 34, 35, and 36 of the written statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct, sir, that the commander of this JSO unit was actually located there in Trstenik; that is to say, the entire outfit was in Trstenik rather than in Kosovo, is that correct, when you encountered them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I met him in Trstenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you further testified that the RDB chief in nearby Kraljevo became involved in the aftermath of your alteration trying to resolve the same. Just to clarify for people who may not know the geography. Kraljevo is also well outside the borders of Kosovo i Metohija. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise for pausing. I have to pause to give the translators time to catch up with the transcript. Now, I'd like to move on to another matter that you testified about. Relating to the JSO, the special units of the RDB, you have already testified that Rade Markovic confirmed the information you already had from your security organs that he had deployed 30 of Arkan's men on the ground. Is it your understanding that they were deployed on the ground with the JSO?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, he didn't use the term -- the wording that he deployed them in the territory of Kosovo. He sent them to the territory of Kosovo. And I don't know who else was in Kosovo Polje, where they were. There were some other units there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
